_**Desis bobmarleyi**_ is an underwater spider species found in the shores of north eastern Queensland, Australia. It is known to build air chambers from silk. _D. bobmarleyi_ is named in honour of the Jamaican singer-songwriter Bob Marley.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-BaehRaveHarm17-1) As an intertidal species the name was inspired by Marley's song "High Tide or Low Tide".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2) In April 2018 the World Register of Marine Species named it one of the top 10 most remarkable species discovered in 2017.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2) The spider is an araneomorph. _D. bobmarleyi_ is a recent discovery, which is important to note when examining its data. Additionally, because it is part of the genus _Desis_, it is considered a fully aquatic animal which is interesting because of its evolutionary history. The trnL2 and trnN genes, which are seen in marine spiders that are a part of the genus, must have experienced some kind of rearrangement that allowed for the development of its current traits._[citation needed_] The long hairs on its legs and abdomen trap an air bubble which allows it to breathe while submerged.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2)

Abstract  
Spiders of the genus Desis Walckenaer, 1837 (Araneae: Desidae) are water-adapted spiders and live in the intertidal zone on reefs, marine debris and under rocks. Here, we describe a new intertidal species from tropical Queensland and name it after Bob Marley, whose song “High Tide or Low Tide” inspired us as it lives in a “high tide low tide” habitat. We also re-describe a close morphological relative, Desis vorax L. Koch, 1872 from Sāmoa. This species was described some 150 years ago from the Godeffroy Collection which holds the oldest major collection of Australasian and Pacific spiders, now mainly hosted in the Centre of Natural History in Hamburg (CeNak). A third species, Desis hartmeyeri Simon, 1909, was described from juvenile specimens only and is considered a nomen dubium.

_**Desis bobmarleyi**_ is an underwater spider species found in the shores of north eastern Queensland, Australia. It is known to build air chambers from silk. _D. bobmarleyi_ is named in honour of the Jamaican singer-songwriter Bob Marley.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-BaehRaveHarm17-1) As an intertidal species the name was inspired by Marley's song "High Tide or Low Tide".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2) In April 2018 the World Register of Marine Species named it one of the top 10 most remarkable species discovered in 2017.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2) The spider is an araneomorph. _D. bobmarleyi_ is a recent discovery, which is important to note when examining its data. Additionally, because it is part of the genus _Desis_, it is considered a fully aquatic animal which is interesting because of its evolutionary history. The trnL2 and trnN genes, which are seen in marine spiders that are a part of the genus, must have experienced some kind of rearrangement that allowed for the development of its current traits._[citation needed_] The long hairs on its legs and abdomen trap an air bubble which allows it to breathe while submerged.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_bobmarleyi#cite_note-ABCApr18-2)

## Material and methods
Recent specimens of _Desis_ were collected and stored in 75% EtOH. All specimens were examined in 75% EtOH using a Leica M 205 A microscope. The female genitalia were dissected, cleared with Pancreatin (Álvarez-Padilla and Hormiga 2007) at room temperature and then imaged. # _Desis galapagoensis_
_**Desis galapagoensis**_ is a species of spider in the genus _Desis_, and the family Desidae.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_galapagoensis#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_galapagoensis#cite_note-2) The species is found on Floreana Island.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desis_galapagoensis#cite_note-3)
